title: Explain One-to-One, One-to-Many, Many-to-One, and Many-to-Many relationships in DB design.
shortTitle: Explain One-to-One, One-to-Many, Many-to-One, and Many-to-Many relationships in DB design.

s1_definition.profdef: Relationship cardinality describes how many rows in one table can associate with rows in another. One-to-one means each row on each side relates to at most one row on the other, typically modeled by a shared or unique foreign key. One-to-many and its mirror many-to-one mean one parent row relates to many child rows while each child relates to one parent, modeled by a foreign key on the child side. Many-to-many means rows on both sides can relate to many rows on the other and is modeled with a junction table holding two foreign keys.

A customer can hold many products like a savings account, a credit card, and a loan, and each product type is held by many customers — that is many-to-many, which the bank records in a separate holdings table pairing customer with product.

s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Relationship cardinality describes how many rows in one table can associate with rows in another. One-to-one means each row on each side relates to at most one row on the other, typically modeled by a shared or unique foreign key. One-to-many and its mirror many-to-one mean one parent row relates to many child rows while each child relates to one parent, modeled by a foreign key on the child side. Many-to-many means rows on both sides can relate to many rows on the other and is modeled with a junction table holding two foreign keys.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, each account has exactly one KYC record and each KYC record belongs to exactly one account — that is one-to-one. One account has many transactions, and each transaction belongs to one account — that is one-to-many from the account's side and many-to-one from the transaction's side, two views of the same link. A customer can hold many products like a savings account, a credit card, and a loan, and each product type is held by many customers — that is many-to-many, which the bank records in a separate holdings table pairing customer with product.

**One line to remember:** One-to-one is a unique foreign key, one-to-many and many-to-one are the two views of a foreign key on the child, and many-to-many needs a junction table with two foreign keys.

sections.s2_technical:
A one-to-one relationship means a row on each side maps to at most one row on the other. You model it by putting a foreign key on one table that references the other and making that foreign key unique, which forbids a second child from pointing at the same parent. One-to-one is used to split a table for good reasons: separating rarely used or large columns, isolating sensitive data like KYC details under tighter access control, or extending a table without altering it. Often the child shares the same primary key value as the parent.

A one-to-many relationship means one parent row relates to many child rows. You model it by putting a foreign key on the child table referencing the parent's primary key, with no uniqueness on that foreign key so many children can share the same parent. This is the most common relationship in any schema: one account to many transactions, one customer to many accounts, one order to many line items. Many-to-one is not a different mechanism — it is the same relationship seen from the child's perspective. From the account you look one-to-many at its transactions; from a transaction you look many-to-one at its account. The foreign key lives on the "many" side in both descriptions.

A many-to-many relationship means rows on both sides can relate to many rows on the other. You cannot model this with a single foreign key because neither side can hold a list of references in a normalized design. Instead you introduce a junction table, also called a bridge or associative table, which has one foreign key to each side, and whose primary key is usually the composite of those two foreign keys. For example a customer-product holdings table pairs a customer id with a product id, so one customer can appear with many products and one product with many customers. The junction table is also the natural place to store attributes of the relationship itself, such as the date a customer acquired a product or their credit limit on a card. A senior nuance is that in JPA these map to annotations — `@OneToOne`, `@OneToMany` with `@ManyToOne` on the owning side, and `@ManyToMany` or, better, an explicit entity for the junction table when it carries its own attributes. Another nuance is indexing: the foreign keys in junction tables and on the many side should be indexed for join performance, and you should decide the cascade and delete behavior deliberately, for example whether removing a customer removes their holdings rows.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India keeps sensitive KYC details separate from the main account record for access control, and each account has exactly one KYC record. This is exactly a one-to-one relationship with a unique foreign key.

Problem 2 — One account has many transactions, and each transaction belongs to exactly one account. This is exactly a one-to-many relationship from the account and a many-to-one from the transaction, modeled by a foreign key on transactions.

Problem 3 — A customer can hold many products and each product is held by many customers, and the bank records extra facts like the acquisition date on each holding. This is exactly a many-to-many relationship modeled with a junction table.

The mini-project creates all four shapes — accounts to kyc (one-to-one), accounts to transactions (one-to-many and many-to-one), and customers to products via a holdings junction (many-to-many) — and a demo that inserts and queries each to show the cardinalities in action.
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build and run
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -jar target/relationships-demo-1.0.0.jar

# See the many-to-many join directly
psql -d bankdb -c "SELECT c.full_name, p.name FROM holdings h
  JOIN customers c USING (customer_id) JOIN products p USING (product_id) ORDER BY c.full_name;"
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input: accounts with transactions and KYC, and customers holding products through the holdings junction.

Step 1 (one-to-many): The demo asks for all transactions of SAV2001. The query filters the transactions table by account_id and returns TXN-1 and TXN-2. One account produced many transactions, each carrying the single account id — that same link read from a transaction is many-to-one.

Step 2 (one-to-one): The demo asks whether SAV2001 is KYC verified. Because account_kyc uses the account id as its own primary key, there is at most one KYC row per account, so the lookup returns exactly one value, true.

Step 3 (many-to-many): The demo asks for customer 1's products. The query joins holdings to products, finding two holdings rows for customer 1, and returns Savings and Credit Card. Customer 1 relates to many products.

Step 4 (many-to-many mirror): The demo asks for customer 2's products and gets Savings and Home Loan. The product Savings is held by both customers, proving the relationship is many on both sides, which only the junction table can represent.

```text
Feb 14,2026 11:20:00 INFO  RelationshipDao - SAV2001 has 2 transactions (one-to-many)
Feb 14,2026 11:20:00 INFO  RelationshipDemo - SAV2001 KYC verified? true
Feb 14,2026 11:20:00 INFO  RelationshipDao - Customer 1 holds [Savings, Credit Card] (many-to-many)
Feb 14,2026 11:20:00 INFO  RelationshipDao - Customer 2 holds [Savings, Home Loan] (many-to-many)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  ── One-to-One ──
  accounts(SAV2001) ──1:1── account_kyc(account_id=SAV2001)   (shared/unique PK)

  ── One-to-Many / Many-to-One ──
  accounts(SAV2001) ──1 : many──→ transactions(TXN-1, TXN-2)
       (from account: one-to-many)   (from a txn: many-to-one; FK on the many side)

  ── Many-to-Many (needs a junction) ──
  customers        holdings (junction)        products
   Rajesh(1) ─┐    (1,SAV)(1,CC)              ┌─ Savings(SAV)
              ├──→ (2,SAV)(2,LOAN) ←──────────┤  Credit Card(CC)
   Priya(2) ──┘    PK(customer_id,product_id) └─ Home Loan(LOAN)
   both hold Savings → only a junction table can express this
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — Cardinality Patterns ═══

  ┌─ How each relationship is modeled ───────────────────────────────┐
  │ One-to-One:   unique/shared FK (child PK = parent PK)             │
  │ One-to-Many:  FK on the MANY side, no uniqueness                 │
  │ Many-to-One:  same FK, viewed from the child                     │
  │ Many-to-Many: junction table, composite PK of two FKs            │
  │ JPA: @OneToOne / @OneToMany+@ManyToOne / @ManyToMany (or entity) │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Entity Diagram ─────────────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌──────────────┐ 1   1 ┌──────────────┐     ┌──────────────┐ 1 * ┌────────────┐
  │ accounts     │◆─────→│ account_kyc  │     │ customers    │◇───→│ holdings   │
  │ + id PK      │       │ account_id PK│     │ + cust_id PK │     │ cust_id FK │
  └──────┬───────┘       │  = accounts  │     └──────────────┘     │ prod_id FK │
     1   │ *             └──────────────┘     ┌──────────────┐ 1 * │ PK(both)   │
         ▼                                     │ products     │◇───→│ acquired_on│
  ┌──────────────┐                             │ + prod_id PK │     └────────────┘
  │ transactions │                             └──────────────┘
  │ account_id FK│  (many side holds the FK)
  └──────────────┘

  Contract for productsOf(customerId):
    Pre:  customerId exists
    Post: returns every product linked via a holdings row (0..many)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Relationship cardinality is simply how many rows on one side can associate with rows on the other, and there are three underlying shapes. A one-to-one relationship means each row on each side maps to at most one row on the other, and you model it by putting a foreign key on one table that references the other and making that foreign key unique, often by letting the child share the parent's primary key. You use one-to-one to split off sensitive or rarely used columns, such as keeping KYC details in a separate table with tighter access control.

A one-to-many relationship means one parent relates to many children, and you model it by putting a foreign key on the child side referencing the parent's primary key, with no uniqueness so many children can share one parent. Many-to-one is not a different mechanism; it is the same relationship viewed from the child. From an account you look one-to-many at its transactions, and from a transaction you look many-to-one at its account — the foreign key lives on the many side either way. This is the most common relationship in any schema.

A many-to-many relationship means both sides can relate to many rows on the other, and a single foreign key cannot express it, so you introduce a junction table with one foreign key to each side and usually a composite primary key of the two. The junction table is also where you store attributes of the relationship itself, like the date a customer acquired a product. At the National Bank of India, accounts to KYC is one-to-one with a shared primary key, accounts to transactions is one-to-many with the foreign key on transactions, and customers to products is many-to-many through a holdings junction that also records the acquisition date — and the product Savings being held by two different customers is exactly why only a junction table works. The line I always state is that one-to-one is a unique foreign key, one-to-many and many-to-one are the two views of a foreign key on the child, and many-to-many needs a junction table with two foreign keys.
